      How this is scored

      The scale

      Critical, Elevated and Managed are Green Dolphin’s sector attention levels, built for board discussion. They are not supervisory ratings and do not represent the view of any regulator, and they describe external pressure on a sector, not any firm’s risk.

      How a level is set

      Each quarter, for each sector and sub-risk, we ask three questions of the cited evidence: has a regulator, official body or Parliament moved on this in the quarter (a rule, review, finding, designation, alert or statement); does the move bear on firms in this sector at the scale we serve; and does the acute part of the evidence belong to this sub-risk or a neighbouring one. Critical means acute and on the agenda now; Elevated means needing closer attention than routine; Managed means within routine oversight. The trend within a level is separate from the level: Rising when the evidence is building, Holding when it is steady, Intensifying when regulators moved on it more than once in the quarter. An arrow beside a family marks a change of level since the last edition where the comparison is direct (see Comparability below); the colour shows only the current level. Families are grouped by level and are not ranked against each other.

      Earlier editions also showed a single composite number out of five. It was an editorial index, not a measured score, and from the Q4 2026 edition it is replaced by the counts of families at each level and the list of what changed. Archived editions keep their published number for the record.

      Sources and their types

      Every sector claim is cited to a primary source: the FCA, PRA, Bank of England, NCSC, Information Commission, PSR or UK Parliament, with UK Finance and CMORG as sector bodies. Each source is labelled by type: a binding rule, a supervisory expectation, official guidance, a reported finding, an official statement or decision, a proposal or consultation, or voluntary sector practice. A reported finding or a voluntary document is not a new requirement, and the text says so. The level and the narrative are Green Dolphin’s interpretation.

      The name and the scope

      Until September 2026 this was published as the Digital Risk Radar. The Q4 2026 edition renamed it the Operational Risk Radar, and this relaunch edition restructures it from eight domains into ten principal families and fifty sub-risks: Resilience & External Disruption; Third Parties & Supply Chain; Fraud & Financial Crime; Customer & Conduct; Legal, Regulatory & Compliance; Data, AI & Models; Change & Transformation; People, Culture & Governance; Processes & Reporting; Technology & Cyber. The catalogue is a working structure for board discussion, not a complete operational-risk taxonomy and not a compliance framework. Archived editions keep the eight domains and the name they were published under.

      Families, sub-risks and how a family level is set

      In the interface, sub-risks are called topics. Each sub-risk is assessed for each sector. A family level is the highest level among its assessed sub-risks, and the family view names the sub-risk or sub-risks that set it, with how many of the family’s sub-risks were assessed. A family is never scored on its own, and a sub-risk is not downgraded because the sector is small or the quarter was quiet; equally, a level is not raised to make a quarter look eventful. For each sub-risk the Radar states separately whether it is operationally relevant to the sector, which instruments apply to it and with what scope, whether there was a development this quarter, and whether the evidence was sufficient to assess it.

      Questions by role

      Each topic carries one leading question for each of the six roles. Where two roles share the same responsibility for a topic, they share the same question and the panel says so; a different wording for its own sake would not help the reader. Additional probes sit in the follow-ups rather than in the leading question.

      Evidence states

      Current development: a verified publication or event inside the quarter bears on the topic; where a rule commenced in the quarter but was published earlier, both dates are shown. Standing coverage: no new publication in the quarter after a documented scan of the evidence base; the level rests on established sources and the scan note says so. Not assessed: the evidence was insufficient to form a view; the gap is explained, and the topic is excluded from the family level. Not assessed is distinct from not applicable, which means the topic does not apply to the sector. Limited applicability means the topic applies to part of the sector or part of a firm’s activity; it is assessed, with the scope stated, rather than left out. A material topic is not left unassessed merely because nothing was published about it in the quarter.

      Comparability with earlier editions

      Movement is shown against the most recent archived quarter, family by family, under three rules. Where a former domain maps wholly to one family (Third Parties, Customer & Conduct, Resilience), the family compares directly and an arrow marks a change of level. Where a family is wider than the domain it took over (Technology & Cyber from Cyber and Technology; Data, AI & Models from AI; Fraud & Financial Crime from Fraud; Legal, Regulatory & Compliance from Regulatory), it is marked Regrouped and the comparison is made at the inherited sub-risk, so a wider scope cannot read as a deterioration. Where there is nothing to compare with (Change & Transformation; People, Culture & Governance; Processes & Reporting), the family is marked New this edition, which means new to the Radar’s coverage and never a newly emerging exposure. Counts of levels across editions are different populations and are not compared. The Q1 2027 edition will be the first with a like-for-like ten-family comparison. Archived editions are drawn with the eight-domain geometry and text they were published with.

      Mapping from the eight domains. Cyber & Data Security → Technology & Cyber (attack, access, vulnerabilities, recovery) and Data, AI & Models (privacy and data security). Technology & IT → Technology & Cyber (availability, legacy), Change & Transformation (migration and go-live) and Processes & Reporting (payments). AI & Emerging Tech → Data, AI & Models. Third Party & Supply Chain → Third Parties & Supply Chain. Customer & Conduct Risk → Customer & Conduct. Fraud & Financial Crime → Fraud & Financial Crime (widened to money laundering, sanctions, bribery and market abuse) and Customer & Conduct (claims handling standards). Regulatory & Compliance → Legal, Regulatory & Compliance, with reporting accuracy in Processes & Reporting. Operational Resilience → Resilience & External Disruption, with cyber recovery in Technology & Cyber.

      Source policy

      Evidence comes from regulators and official bodies, Parliament and the courts, with UK Finance and TLP:CLEAR CMORG material as sector bodies labelled voluntary practice. Consultancy publications and professional-body guidance are not used as evidence. From this edition, Building Societies Association and Cifas material is no longer used in the active edition’s evidence; archived editions are unchanged. Where Green Dolphin draws an inference beyond what a source says, the text labels it as our read.

      Glossary

      CTP
      Critical Third Party: a supplier designated by HM Treasury as critical to the UK financial system, now under direct regulator oversight.
      Impact tolerance
      The maximum disruption a firm's board has decided an important business service can bear.
      PQC
      Post-quantum cryptography: encryption designed to withstand future quantum computers. The NCSC roadmap runs to 2035.
      APP fraud
      Authorised push payment fraud: a customer is tricked into sending money to a criminal. Reimbursement rules have applied since October 2024.
      CAF
      The NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, the UK baseline for assessing cyber resilience.
      CoP
      Confirmation of Payee: the name-check made before a payment is sent.
      FCA, PRA, Bank of England
      The Financial Conduct Authority (conduct regulator), the Prudential Regulation Authority (safety and soundness, part of the Bank of England) and the Bank itself, whose Financial Policy Committee (FPC) watches stability and whose Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate.
      FOS
      The Financial Ombudsman Service, which settles complaints between customers and firms.
      FSCS
      The Financial Services Compensation Scheme, which pays customers when a firm fails.
      ICO / Information Commission
      The UK data-protection regulator; the Information Commissioner’s Office became the Information Commission on 30 September 2026.
      MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS
      Public knowledge bases of the techniques attackers use against systems (ATT&CK) and against AI (ATLAS).
      NCSC
      The National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, the UK’s technical authority on cyber security.
      PSR
      The Payment Systems Regulator; the Bill before Parliament transfers its functions to the FCA.
      RTGS, CHAPS, ISO 20022
      The Bank of England’s settlement system, the UK’s high-value payment system, and the messaging standard both are moving to.
      SM&CR
      The Senior Managers and Certification Regime: named senior managers are individually accountable for defined responsibilities.
      SS, PS, CP
      A PRA Supervisory Statement, a Policy Statement (final rules) and a Consultation Paper (proposed rules).
      TLP
      Traffic Light Protocol: the sharing marking on sector documents. Only TLP:CLEAR material is cited here.

      From the founders
      Why we built the radar
      
  
      
    
      
      
      
      
        
        
      The Radar came out of the boardrooms we work in. I kept seeing the same gap: capable boards, serious about digital risk, with no clear, cited view of what was shifting across their sector, and no time to read every regulator publication to build one. So we built the thing we kept wishing was already on the table. It is free, it needs no login, and it asks for no personal details, because the point was never to capture anyone. One rule holds it together: if a claim cannot be traced to a primary source, it does not appear. If the Radar helps your next meeting open from the evidence rather than a debate about sources, it has done its job.
      
        
      Paul O’LearyFounder and Director · Green Dolphin (TCCR)

      Guide
      How to read this radar
      
  
      
  
      The key in full
      
  
      Levels. Critical: acute, on the board agenda this quarter. Elevated: needs closer attention than routine. Managed: within routine oversight. Levels are Green Dolphin’s assessment of external attention on the sector, not a rating of any firm. A family sits at the level of its highest assessed topic.
      
  
      Movement. Rising, Holding or Intensifying describe the trend inside a level (Intensifying when regulators moved on it more than once in the quarter). ▲▼ marks a change of level since the last edition where a family compares directly with its former domain; Regrouped and New this edition mark families that cannot be compared that way. Colour shows only the current level.
      
  
      Evidence. Current development: a verified publication or event in the quarter. Standing coverage: assessed on established sources after a documented scan found no significant new development. Not assessed: left out of the family level, with the gap explained. Limited applicability: assessed, with the scope stated.
      
    
      What it shows. Ten operational-risk families for the sector you choose, each opening a short list of topics, with a sector attention level: Critical (act now), Elevated (prepare: needs closer attention than routine) or Managed (monitor), and a trend within the level (Rising, Holding, Intensifying). Closer to the centre is a higher level. ▲ or ▼ on a label means the level changed since the last edition.
      
    
      Levels describe external pressure. They are Green Dolphin’s read of what regulators, official bodies and Parliament have done and said in the quarter, for firms in your sector. They are not a rating of your firm.
      
    
      Open a topic. Choose a starting topic, click or tap a signal, or pick from the list. The panel stays open until you choose another or go back. It starts with the level in plain terms, one leading question for your role, the evidence to request and why it matters now. Supporting detail sits in three groups underneath: prepare the discussion (follow-ups, weaker and stronger answers, further questions), evidence and examples (the main official sources, a dated example, all sources), and further detail (Green Dolphin’s fuller interpretation, a figure, proportionality, technical mappings).
      
    
      Sector and role. Sector sets the levels, text and examples. Role sets the leading question and one evidence request per risk; the other evidence items are shared across roles.
      
    
      Tailoring. Purpose, role and sector change which questions and starting topics you see, never the sector levels. Firm size changes only the proportionality text and the calibration note. “Add to meeting preparation” collects up to three topics for the meeting brief and does not change colours or levels. Archived editions show what was published then, and downloads follow the edition you have selected. Your choices are stored in this browser; the general share link carries none of them, the tailored link carries the settings described beside it, and feedback you choose to send goes to Green Dolphin.
      
    
      What this is. A free, cited starting point for a board or committee conversation. Not advice, and not a substitute for your own risk register.
